triage_context.environment: Internet-facing web service: public Django/DRF API; HTTP + uploaded scanner reports untrusted; low-priv roles (Upload/Writer) can upload, Maintainer/Owner configure integrations & author Rego; cross-product access is a breach; external IdP reaches OIDC.
threat_model: Compliance-scoped data exposure (integration secrets / crypto keys)

findings.title: Issue-tracker API key returned in product API responses to any user with read (View) permission
preconditions: Attacker is authenticated (valid session/token; endpoint enforces IsAuthenticated, anonymous is rejected)

Attacker holds at least the lowest Reader role on the target product, granting object-level Product_View via membership (UserHasProductPermission.has_object_permission -> check_object_permission with get_permission=Permissions.Product_View)
An issue_tracker_api_key is actually configured (non-empty) on that product; the field is a blank-allowed CharField, so a product with no issue-tracker integration has no secret to leak

Attacker issues GET /api/products/{id}/ for a product they can view (ProductViewSet retrieve uses ProductSerializer whose Meta.exclude omits issue_tracker_api_key, with no write_only/to_representation masking)
findings.threat_match: Compliance-scoped data exposure (integration secrets / crypto keys): the product's Jira/GitHub/GitLab issue_tracker_api_key is returned in cleartext to the lowest Reader role, exposing an integration secret to a role meant to have read-only visibility, not secret access. The leaked token also enables lateral movement into the connected issue tracker.
findings.rationale:
Confirmed by reading source, not the description. serializers_product.py:295 ProductSerializer.Meta uses exclude=["is_product_group","members","authorization_group_members","observation_notification_statuses"] and inherits fields="__all__" from ProductCoreSerializer (line 70). models.py:101 defines issue_tracker_api_key = CharField(max_length=255, blank=True) in cleartext, and it is NOT in any exclude list and has no write_only declaration. No to_representation override pops it: ProductCoreSerializer.to_representation (lines 123-129) only sets observation_notification_status_list; the api_key references at lines 385/390 are write-path validation only. Caller trace: views_product.py:143 ProductViewSet.serializer_class = ProductSerializer with permission_classes=(IsAuthenticated, UserHasProductPermission); get_serializer_class (163-167) returns ProductListSerializer for list (which ALSO includes the field via the same exclude at line 256) and ProductSerializer for retrieve. permissions.py:28-35 UserHasProductPermission.has_object_permission gates GET on Permissions.Product_View, which every product role including the lowest Viewer/Reader holds (roles_permissions.py grants Product_View at lines 189/213/229/252/302). Stress-test of protections: searched for write_only, extra_kwargs, to_representation masking, and auth gates on the field — none exist on this path. Decisive contrast: the project's own ApiConfigurationSerializer.to_representation (import_observations/api/serializers.py:111-117) explicitly pops api_key unless the caller has Api_Configuration_Edit ("Only users who can edit an API Configuration are allowed to see the API key"), proving secret-masking is the intended design and the Product serializer's omission is a deviation, not intent. So a low-priv read-only Viewer can GET /api/products/{id}/ and receive the cleartext Jira/GitHub/GitLab issue-tracker token (and the notification webhook URLs, similarly unmasked). No exclusion applies: concrete exploit with a real read path returning a real cross-integration secret (not rule 13 missing-hardening); authz/sensitive-data class in a safe language (not rule 4); not test/dead/intended. Confidence below 1.0 only because I did not execute to observe the literal HTTP response body, but the static path is unambiguous.

Confirmed in source: serializers_product.py:295 ProductSerializer.Meta uses exclude=[is_product_group, members, authorization_group_members, observation_notification_statuses] which does NOT exclude issue_tracker_api_key (models.py:101, a CharField). No write_only and no to_representation masking; the only handling of the field (lines 385/390) is write-time validation. ProductViewSet (views_product.py:143) uses ProductSerializer for retrieve and gates only on IsAuthenticated + object-level Product_View. Pure precondition math = authenticated + 1 config precondition -> MEDIUM. Step 3 threat-model match (integration-secret/compliance-scoped exposure to an under-privileged role, plus lateral-movement potential of the leaked token) raises one step to HIGH. Not unauthenticated and not cross-tenant by itself (object permission requires product membership), so it stops at HIGH, not beyond. Scanner claimed HIGH and is correct on outcome and root location; its only error is the mechanism description (it said fields=__all__ inherited from ProductCoreSerializer; the real mechanism is an exclude list that omits the field) — same result, so +1 (roughly right, slightly imprecise rationale).

findings.title: Stored XSS via SBOM component names assigned to element.innerHTML before mermaid sanitization
preconditions: Attacker holds an authenticated account with at least Upload/Writer role on a product (low-priv, but explicitly an available role per the threat model).

Attacker uploads a crafted CycloneDX SBOM (or OSV report) whose component name / bom-ref contains an HTML payload, e.g. a component named ''. The CycloneDX parser concatenates these names verbatim into origin_component_dependencies as 'A --> B' lines (cyclone_dx/parser.py:259, dependencies.py:24) with no escaping.

A victim opens the observation detail view and the 'Component dependency graph' is rendered (ObservationShowOrigins.tsx:94 -> MermaidDependencies useEffect), where element.innerHTML = createMermaidGraph(dependencies) (line 111) parses the attacker markup before mermaid.run(). No DOMPurify; component names are interpolated raw at lines 83-84.

For privilege-escalation/tenant impact the rendering victim must be a higher-privileged user (Maintainer/Owner) with access to the attacker's product; SecObserve scopes observations per product, so a cross-product victim must already have access to the attacker-controlled product.

MITIGATING: a browser that enforces the app's Content-Security-Policy will not run the inline onerror handler. backend/config/settings/base.py:277 sets script-src 'self' with NO 'unsafe-inline', which per CSP spec blocks inline event-handler execution (the PoC). Exploitation requires that this CSP NOT reach the React SPA document (the middleware applies to Django responses; the SPA is served separately), or an alternate non-inline-script vector.
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (and secondarily tenant-to-tenant data leakage): a low-priv Upload/Writer plants a stored-XSS payload in SBOM-derived component names; if it executes in a Maintainer/Owner session viewing the observation, it can steal session tokens or act as that user. This would justify a one-step raise MEDIUM -> HIGH, but the raise is offset by the strict CSP (script-src 'self', no unsafe-inline) which blocks the inline-handler PoC, so net stays MEDIUM pending confirmation that the SPA actually enforces this CSP.
findings.rationale: Confirmed at Mermaid_Dependencies.tsx:111: `element.innerHTML = createMermaidGraph(dependencies)` executes BEFORE `mermaid.run()` at :112. createMermaidGraph (lines 73,83,84) embeds component names raw into the string with zero HTML escaping (wrapped as `id1("name")` and emitted as raw dependency lines). innerHTML assignment makes the browser HTML-parse the string at assignment time, so a component name like `` fires onerror immediately, independent of mermaid strict-mode sanitization (which only governs mermaid's own rendered SVG output, not the pre-assignment parse). Data flow is fully attacker-controlled and untrusted: first call-site ObservationShowOrigins.tsx:94 passes observation.origin_component_dependencies. Backend builds this from uploaded CycloneDX SBOM component name/version: cyclone_dx/parser.py:208 reads `name=component_data.get("name","")` raw; _translate_package_id (parser.py:445-454) forms `name:version`; _get_component_dependencies (parser.py:417-427) joins into the dependency string; Observation.origin_component_dependencies (core/models.py:285) and Component.component_name (models.py:553) are plain CharField/TextField with NO validators stripping HTML metacharacters; serializers_observation.py:178 exposes it unescaped. Per ENVIRONMENT a low-priv Upload/Writer role can upload SBOMs, and the rendered observation is viewable by others (cross-product/cross-user breach). No DOMPurify or sanitize exists in frontend/src; no dangerouslySetInnerHTML escape but the direct innerHTML sink is equivalent. Exclusion analysis: Rule 14 does NOT apply — this is precisely the raw-HTML escape hatch (direct element.innerHTML assignment) that rule 14 carves out as still-valid XSS, not auto-escaped JSX. Rule 9 does NOT apply — XSS is inherently a client-side class, so client code is the correct locus. Not test/dead (rule 2), not intended design (rule 3), not DoS (rule 1). findings.title: Committed default DJANGO_SECRET_KEY in shipped prod compose files
preconditions: Operator deploys using this compose file WITHOUT overriding SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, so the committed literal NxYPEF5l... becomes the effective Django SECRET_KEY (config/settings/base.py:29 reads DJANGO_SECRET_KEY with no fallback, so the value comes from the compose default).
Attacker obtains the committed literal — trivially satisfied for a public repo, but still a distinct precondition.

The deployment relies on a SECRET_KEY-signed mechanism that an attacker can leverage: Django session cookies, signed cookies, or password-reset token generator. Primary API auth is JWT signed by a separate DB-stored random JWT_Secret (jwt_authentication.py:31/69, HS256), so forging JWTs is NOT possible via this key.
Attacker has network reach to the web endpoint that consumes the forged session cookie / reset token and a target account whose session or reset flow can be forged.

Integration secrets / crypto keys are NOT in scope of this key — they are protected by the separate FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY (base.py:432), so the compliance-scoped-data-exposure threat does not apply to SECRET_KEY.
findings.threat_match: Partial: maps to "Privilege escalation to admin" only if session cookies / password-reset tokens are the live auth path and an admin account can be targeted via a forged signed token. Does NOT map to compliance-scoped data exposure (integration secrets use the separate FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY) nor to the JWT-based primary auth. Match is conditional and bounded; at most a one-step consideration.
findings.rationale:
Verified the finding directly. docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:85 ships DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: ${SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY:-NxYPEF5lNGgk3yonndjSbwP77uNJxOvfKTjF5aVBqsHktNlf1wfJHHvJ8iifk32r} — a real, publicly committed 64-char literal. The same literal is the default across every prod compose file (prod-postgres.yml:85, prod-mysql.yml:85, prod-test.yml:52) plus the dev/test files. Backwards trace: config/settings/base.py:29 reads SECRET_KEY = env("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY") with NO in-code default, so the committed compose literal is the effective production SECRET_KEY whenever an operator fails to export SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY. SECRET_KEY signs Django sessions, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens and other signed values; a publicly-known value lets a remote unauthenticated attacker forge session cookies and signed tokens against any default deployment — a concrete auth-bypass primitive, not a theoretical one, and the service is internet-facing.

Protections hunted and stress-tested: (a) No fail-closed startup guard — grep of settings/ and bin/ shows no check that rejects an empty or default SECRET_KEY (only an unrelated HUEY_IMMEDIATE ValueError at base.py:438); the value is consumed raw. (b) Docs (installation.md:32-37, configuration.md:23) merely advise that SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY "should be changed" — an advisory note, not enforcement, and it explicitly acknowledges the default is a secret left live. (c) The Helm chart (values.yaml:165, README) correctly sources the key from a required secretKeyRef with no committed fallback — confirming the maintainers know the value must be operator-supplied, which makes the compose committed default the gap, not intended design. (d) THREAT_MODEL.md (T2/T3) independently flags this committed default as a critical, partially_mitigated risk.

Exclusion rules: Rule 13 (missing-hardening-only) does NOT apply — this is a concrete known-secret enabling token/session forgery, not absent hardening. Rule 8 (trusted operator input) does NOT apply — the secret is committed in the shipped repo, and the threat is precisely the operator NOT overriding it. Rule 3 (intended design) does NOT apply — an out-of-box convenience default in dev files is one thing, but shipping the identical secret in the *prod* compose files with no fail-closed guard is the classic hardcoded-default-secret weakness (CWE-798/CWE-1188). HIGH severity is justified for an internet-facing public API.

Although the secret is readable by an unauthenticated remote attacker (public repo) and at first looks like the 0-precondition/unauth HIGH row, exploitation is gated by at least two real preconditions: (1) the operator must fail to override SO_DJANGO_SECRET_KEY — the compose value is only a fallback default, and any prod deploy is expected to set it; and (2) the deployment must actually rely on a SECRET_KEY-signed surface reachable by the attacker. Crucially, the primary API auth uses a separate, randomly generated DB-stored JWT secret (jwt_authentication.py), so this key cannot forge API tokens — impact is bounded to Django sessions, signed cookies, and password-reset tokens. By STEP 2, with 1-2 preconditions the authenticated/effective-precondition column caps this at MEDIUM; the unauth-access column would suggest HIGH, and the rule takes the LOWER, i.e. MEDIUM. STEP 3 allows at most a one-step raise for a conditional privilege-escalation match, which would only restore HIGH if the impact path were unconditional — it is not, so MEDIUM holds. The scanner's HIGH is inflated by one level (the JWT bounding the verifier itself noted), hence -1. Verdict needs_manual_test because exploitability hinges on whether the live deployment overrides the key and whether session/reset flows are actually in use — a runtime check, not a static one. Real and worth fixing (rotate + force-override), but not a clean unauth-RCE/HIGH.

findings.title: Committed default FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY in shipped prod compose defeats all at-rest field encryption
preconditions: Operator did NOT set SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY and accepted the committed default DtlkqVb3... — docs (configuration.md:24, installation.md) mark FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY as 'mandatory' with key-generation instructions, so a correctly configured deployment overrides it; the value is a ${VAR:-default} fallback, not a forced hardcoded secret.

Attacker obtains the at-rest ciphertext: a database dump, backup, DB credential, or other DB-level/backend access. The committed key alone is useless without the encrypted column values stored in the DB. There is NO path from the public HTTP/DRF surface to the DB contents.

For token forgery specifically: a JWT_Secret singleton row exists in the DB (created on first auth use) so JWT_Secret.secret ciphertext is present to decrypt; secret is signed/verified in jwt_authentication.py:31/69.
Attacker position is insider / DB-adjacent (stolen backup, separate DB-exposure bug, or operator/infra access) — not the modeled external HTTP/upload/OIDC attacker.
findings.threat_match: Maps to "Compliance-scoped data exposure (integration secrets / crypto keys)" and the codebase's own THREAT_MODEL.md T3 (secret exposure by deployment default, attacker=insider, status=partially_mitigated). Once the DB is in hand the blast radius also touches "Tenant-to-tenant data leakage" and "Privilege escalation to admin" via forged superuser JWTs. Threat-model match raises the derived LOW by one step to MEDIUM.
findings.rationale:
Verified line 86 verbatim: FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY defaults to the committed public Fernet key DtlkqVb3wlaVdJK_BU-3mB4wwuuf8xx8YNInajiJ7GU= via ${SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-...}. Backwards trace: base.py:432 reads env("FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY") with NO validation that it differs from the shipped default and NO fail-closed boot check (THREAT_MODEL.md:112 lists such a check as still-missing). The key drives django-encrypted-model-fields for every EncryptedCharField, including the security-critical ones: JWT_Secret.secret (access_control/models.py:104) and integration credentials api_key/basic_auth_password (import_observations/models.py:44,49). Concrete exploit: the default is identical across all prod compose files (prod-postgres/mysql/test); an operator who does not override SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY runs a world-known key, so anyone with the public repo + a DB dump can decrypt JWT_Secret, recover the JWT signing secret, and forge auth tokens for any user (cross-product breach per environment). Exclusion rules tested: Rule 8 (trusted operator input) does not apply — the vuln is a committed world-readable default that takes effect on a no-op deploy, which is the hardcoded-secret class, not an operator-supplied value. Rule 13 (missing-hardening, no exploit) does not apply — there is a concrete decrypt-and-forge path. Rule 2 (test/fixture) does not apply — this is a production compose file. The threat model's owner-stated override only affects the one interviewed instance; the finding correctly scores the shipped product default. HIGH severity justified.

Verifier chain is technically correct: FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY (base.py:432) decrypts every EncryptedCharField including JWT_Secret.secret (access_control/models.py:104), and that secret signs/verifies all JWTs (jwt_authentication.py:31,69) plus Api_Configuration.api_key/basic_auth_password — so the default key + DB contents = forge any-user/superuser tokens and recover all integration secrets. But severity derivation: (1) line 86 is a ${SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-default} fallback, and the key is documented as mandatory-to-override (configuration.md:24), so a correct deployment is not affected; (2) exploitation requires DB-at-rest possession, which is not reachable from the public unauthenticated HTTP surface — no demo path. Precondition count 2-3 → MEDIUM/LOW; access level local-only/no-demo-path → LOW; take the lower (LOW), then +1 step for the crypto-key/compliance threat match → MEDIUM. Scanner's HIGH presumes an unauthenticated-remote path that does not exist; inflated by one level (-2). verify_verdict=mitigated: real, but gated by the documented override control and the DB-access requirement. THREAT_MODEL.md also records the owner states their live instance overrides the defaults, scoping this to the self-hosted ecosystem footgun rather than a live remote break.

findings.title: NotificationViewSet.mark_as_viewed uses an unscoped lookup, allowing cross-product notification existence probing
preconditions: Attacker holds a valid authenticated session (any role, including lowest-priv Upload/Writer) — IsAuthenticated is still enforced at the class level; only the object-level product-scope check is bypassed.

Attacker supplies a notification pk to probe. PKs are sequential integers, so enumeration is trivial, but a target id must still be chosen — making this a 1-2 precondition, authenticated-access issue.
findings.threat_match: Tenant-to-tenant data leakage (cross-product). The unscoped get_notification_by_id(pk) lets an authenticated user confirm existence of notifications belonging to products they have no membership in, via the 204 (exists) vs 404 (absent) status differential. Match is real but the leaked datum is only a boolean existence oracle over guessable integer IDs — no notification content, name, or fields are returned, and the side-effect Notification_Viewed row is keyed to the attacker's own user (benign). I therefore do not raise above the mechanically-derived MEDIUM; the disclosure sits at the floor of what counts as leakage.
findings.rationale:
Confirmed by reading the code. views.py:67-69: mark_as_viewed calls get_notification_by_id(pk), which (queries/notification.py:11-15) is unscoped Notification.objects.get(id=...). The product-scoped get_notifications() is wired only into get_queryset() (views.py:37-44), which DRF invokes via get_object() for standard retrieve/destroy. The custom detail action never calls get_object(), so UserHasNotificationPermission.has_object_permission (permissions.py:12) is never triggered. That permission class implements no has_permission method, so request-level checks pass; the only effective gate is IsAuthenticated (views.py:32). Result: any authenticated low-priv user can POST /api/notifications/{pk}/mark_as_viewed/ (registered publicly at api_router.py:105) and observe 204 (notification exists, any product) vs 404 (does not), an enumerable cross-product existence oracle over sequential integer PKs. Cross-product access is defined as a breach in the environment, and IDOR is the named class. No exclusion applies: not DoS, not test/dead code, not intended (the sibling bulk path is scoped, showing the omission is a defect), safe-language IDOR not memory-safety, IDs are sequential PKs not unguessable tokens (rule 15 inapplicable). Impact is genuinely LOW: the endpoint leaks only existence (204/404), returns no notification content, and the write records a view marker keyed to the attacker's own user. Confidence 0.9: code path is unambiguous; only residual is whether some upstream middleware enforces object scoping, which I found no evidence of.

Confirmed IDOR on mark_as_viewed; mechanically MEDIUM, impact is an existence-only oracle.

findings.title: Issue-tracker API key stored unencrypted at rest while sibling credentials use EncryptedCharField
preconditions: A Maintainer/Owner has actually configured an issue tracker on a product, so issue_tracker_api_key is non-empty (field is blank=True and issue_tracker_active defaults False; with no tracker configured there is no secret to leak).
The credential is a live third-party token (GitHub PAT used as Bearer, GitLab PRIVATE-TOKEN, or Jira token) that is currently valid.

Attacker obtains a read channel to the secret: either (a) DB/backup/replica read access from a separate breach (the path in the verifier rationale), or (b) an authenticated session with read access to that product, since ProductSerializer uses fields='__all__' with no write_only/redaction and returns the plaintext field on read.
findings.threat_match: Compliance-scoped data exposure (integration secrets / crypto keys): a live issue-tracker integration credential is stored in cleartext at rest (plain CharField) while every analogous secret in the codebase (Api_Configuration.api_key, basic_auth_password, JWT_Secret.secret) uses EncryptedCharField, and it is also returned on read via the __all__ serializer with no write_only.
findings.rationale:
Verified directly. models.py:101 issue_tracker_api_key is a plain CharField (line 100 username likewise), confirmed by migration core/0012_issue_tracker.py:24-25 which creates a plaintext CharField column. The siblings the finding names are genuinely encrypted: access_control/models.py:104 JWT_Secret.secret, import_observations/models.py:44/49 Api_Configuration.api_key and basic_auth_password all use EncryptedCharField, and FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY is a required setting (config/settings/base.py:432), so encryption is operative — the gap is real, not a no-op. The token is functionally identical to the encrypted ones: a Bearer/PRIVATE-TOKEN credential used to authenticate to GitHub/GitLab/Jira (github_issue_tracker.py:124, gitlab_issue_tracker.py:119, jira_issue_tracker.py:22). Impact is concrete rather than missing-hardening-only (so rule 13 does not apply): (a) the credential sits in cleartext in the DB/backups while every sibling secret is encrypted; (b) the contrast is sharper at the API layer — Api_Configuration's serializer both encrypts AND pops api_key from output for non-editors (import_observations/api/serializers.py:111-117), whereas ProductSerializer (serializers_product.py:272-295) uses an exclude list that does NOT exclude issue_tracker_api_key and has no to_representation masking, so the cleartext token is returned on product reads. This violates the project's own demonstrated design (encrypt-at-rest + restrict read), so it is not intended behavior. No exclusion rule matches. Confidence held at 0.8 because severity hinges partly on threat-model assumptions (DB-at-rest access) but the cleartext-on-read serializer asymmetry independently substantiates a real exposure.

Confirmed: issue_tracker_api_key (core/models.py:101) is a plain CharField holding a live tracker credential (Bearer at github_issue_tracker.py:124, PRIVATE-TOKEN at gitlab_issue_tracker.py:119, Jira token), while comparable secrets use EncryptedCharField (access_control/models.py:104; import_observations/models.py:44,49). Step 1 enumerates 2 preconditions: a tracker must be configured (field is optional/blank), and the attacker needs a read channel — either DB read (downstream of a separate breach) or product-scoped authenticated API read (ProductSerializer fields='__all__', no write_only, so the key is serialized back). Step 2: precondition count 1-2 and the demonstrable channel is authenticated -> MEDIUM; the DB-read framing alone would be LOW (no direct demo path), but the authenticated serializer-return path is a real reachable channel, so the lower-of evaluation lands at MEDIUM rather than LOW. Step 3: matches the compliance-scoped integration-secret threat; the optional one-step bump is not applied because the leaked secret is a third-party tracker token (not SecObserve's own keys) and the realistic path needs product-scoped auth, so it does not cross tenants or escalate privilege on its own. Step 4: claimed HIGH is inflated by one level (-2) — plaintext-at-rest of a live PAT is a genuine weakness, but it is gated behind either a prior DB breach or authenticated product access and exposes a third-party credential, not unauth RCE or direct tenant crossing. Step 5: the at-rest plaintext storage and the __all__ serializer exposure are both certain from source, so exploitable given the stated DB-read precondition (an in-scope breach path in this threat model); only the precise live serializer output would refine the channel.

findings.title: OIDC username claim trusted as the local-account key, enabling account collision/takeover
preconditions: OIDC authentication is enabled in the deployment (env OIDC_USERNAME / OIDC_AUTHORITY / OIDC_CLIENT_ID configured) — config-dependent, not all deployments use OIDC
OIDC_USERNAME is mapped to a mutable/self-asserted claim such as preferred_username rather than an immutable one (sub). If mapped to sub the attack does not work.

Attacker can obtain a validly-signed JWT from the configured IdP whose username claim equals a target user's username — i.e. they control an identity at the IdP and can set/edit that claim (self-registration, editable profile, or a federated second IdP), and the IdP does not enforce uniqueness/immutability of that claim against the target value

A target local or non-OIDC user with the colliding username already exists and is active (e.g. an 'admin' superuser created via createsuperuser); lookup is by username only with no is_oidc_user / issuer / sub binding
findings.threat_match: Privilege escalation to admin (and tenant-to-tenant data leakage): impersonating an existing local 'admin'/superuser username yields full admin; impersonating any other tenant's user yields cross-product access.
findings.rationale:
Confirmed at oidc_authentication.py:79-86. After full JWT validation (signature via IdP JWKS, audience=OIDC_CLIENT_ID, exp/iat/nbf), username=payload.get(os.environ["OIDC_USERNAME"]) is the SOLE key into get_user_by_username (queries/user.py:18-22, plain username lookup). There is NO iss/sub binding and NO is_oidc_user gate before the matched user is returned and authenticated. Crucially, _check_user_change (lines 160-165) retroactively flips is_oidc_user=True and unsets the existing user's password, silently converting a local account during the takeover. Call path: OIDCAuthentication is a DRF default auth class (config/settings/base.py:366); authenticate() at line 26 -> _validate_jwt() at line 44 -> line 79. Collision target exists by default: prod entrypoint (docker/backend/prod/django/entrypoint:39) runs User.objects.create_superuser(ADMIN_USER) creating a password-based superuser (is_oidc_user defaults False), ADMIN_USER default "admin". The vulnerable claim is the SHIPPED DEFAULT: OIDC_USERNAME=preferred_username in docs/integrations/oidc_authentication.md:19, charts/secobserve/values.yaml:190, and docker-compose-dev-keycloak.yml:54. Per OIDC Core, preferred_username is mutable and not guaranteed unique; an attacker with self-service IdP registration can set preferred_username="admin", obtain a validly-signed token for the configured client, and be authenticated as the local superuser — full admin / cross-product breach. Not test/dead (live DRF path), not mere hardening (concrete exploit under default config), not intended (no guard; code converts the local user). Confidence below 1.0 only because exploitability is config-dependent (a unique immutable sub claim defeats it) and requires attacker registration at the trusted IdP — but the default config is exploitable, so it stands as a true positive.

STEP 1 preconditions: (1) OIDC enabled, (2) OIDC_USERNAME mapped to a mutable claim like preferred_username not sub, (3) attacker controls an IdP identity and can set that claim to the victim's username on a JWT the configured IdP will sign, (4) a colliding local/non-OIDC username already exists and is active. findings.title: Teams/Slack webhook URL is user-controlled with no/weak host validation (blind SSRF)

findings.title: Assessment approval gate bypassable by attaching a severity/VEX downgrade to an "In review" status change
preconditions: Attacker is authenticated and holds a role granting Permissions.Observation_Assessment (Writer or higher) on the specific product/product-group containing the target observation (per-product, same-tenant scope).
The target product or its product group has assessments_need_approval=True; if approval is not required, all assessments are AUTO_APPROVED anyway and there is no control to bypass.

Attacker crafts the PATCH .../assessment request to bundle status='In review' together with the field change (severity/priority/vex) they want auto-applied, so the new_status != STATUS_IN_REVIEW clause short-circuits the NEEDS_APPROVAL branch to AUTO_APPROVED.
No prior assessment on that observation is currently in NEEDS_APPROVAL state (views_observation.py:142-146 rejects a new assessment while one awaits approval).
findings.threat_match: None. The impact is a segregation-of-duties / approval-workflow bypass scoped to a product the user already has assessment rights on. It is not tenant-to-tenant leakage (no cross-product access), not privilege escalation to admin (no new permissions gained — the user already holds Observation_Assessment), not secret/crypto-key exposure, and not unauthenticated RCE.
findings.rationale:
Confirmed in source. assessment.py:65-77 computes assessment_status = NEEDS_APPROVAL only if (assessments_need_approval) AND (some field changed) AND (new_status != STATUS_IN_REVIEW), else AUTO_APPROVED. The final AND term means that when new_status == "In review", the whole expression short-circuits to AUTO_APPROVED regardless of which other fields changed. Lines 79-91 then call _update_observation with the full submitted set (severity, status, priority, vex_justification, vex_remediations) applied independently of status. _update_observation (lines 132-158) applies each field on its own condition with no status coupling, and get_current_severity/get_current_vex_* (observation.py:80-81,124-125,156-157) return the assessment_* value first, so a bundled severity/VEX downgrade takes effect live and auto-approved. The serializer ObservationAssessmentSerializer (serializers_observation.py:516-530) accepts severity+status+vex_remediations together with NO cross-field validate() method. First call-site: views_observation.py:148 (the assessment PATCH action), gated only by Permissions.Observation_Assessment; the same flaw is reachable via the bulk path (observations_bulk_actions.py:41/94, same save_assessment). The approval feature is a deliberate separation-of-duties control (docs/usage/assess_observations.md:30-44: the assessment author may not approve their own change; the gate requires a second user). A single Writer/Maintainer/Owner can defeat that second-person approval for severity/VEX downgrades by bundling them with status="In review" in one request, and the result feeds check_security_gate (line 105), so it can flip a product's gate. Not volumetric DoS, not test/dead code, not intended design (the In-review carve-out is meant for pure status-to-In-review transitions, not for waving through bundled severity/VEX downgrades). No exclusion rule applies. Confidence held at 0.85 (not higher) because exploitation requires an already-privileged-but-untrusted-to-self-approve account rather than an anonymous attacker, which slightly tempers impact, but the access-control logic bug itself is unambiguous.

Confirmed logic flaw: assessment.py:65-77 only sets NEEDS_APPROVAL when new_status != STATUS_IN_REVIEW, so bundling status='In review' with a severity/priority/vex change short-circuits to AUTO_APPROVED and _update_observation (line 83) applies the change with no second-party approver — defeating the assessments_need_approval control and the self-approval guard at line 233. Precondition count is 2-3 (authenticated assessment permission on the product + product configured to require approval + crafted request), placing it at the MEDIUM/LOW boundary. Access column: authenticated, same-tenant, requires a specific non-default product configuration → caps at MEDIUM. Impact column: integrity/workflow-control bypass by an actor who already legitimately holds Observation_Assessment; no confidentiality breach, no cross-tenant reach, no privilege gain, no RCE — and it maps to none of the four stated threats, so no upward adjustment is available. Taking the lower of the two evaluations and absent any threat-model bump, derived severity is LOW. The scanner's MEDIUM overstates a same-actor SoD bypass by about one level, hence -2.

findings.title: JSON structure breakout in Slack/Teams notifications via backslash in import-derived observation title
preconditions: Attacker holds an in-tenant Upload or Writer role on a product, enabling import of an observation whose title (or feeds product.name) is attacker-controlled.
A Maintainer/Owner has previously configured an MS Teams or Slack webhook on the product or its product group (notification_ms_teams_webhook / notification_slack_webhook is non-empty).

The notification trigger gate is satisfied: the observation's severity/status/priority match the configured notification thresholds AND it is new or changed, so _create_notification_message actually fires and the payload is POSTed.

The crafted title must contain a backslash-quote sequence so that HTML autoescape (escapes " -> " but not the backslash) followed by replace('"', '\"') yields '\\"' = escaped-backslash + unescaped quote, breaking out of the JSON string.
For impact beyond a malformed/broken notification, the injected JSON must form structure meaningful to the downstream Teams/Slack endpoint (the org's own webhook, same tenant).
findings.threat_match: None of the four stated threats. The injected JSON is POSTed only to the product's own tenant-scoped webhook (Teams/Slack) configured by that tenant's Maintainer/Owner. No cross-tenant path, no privilege escalation, no integration-secret/crypto-key disclosure, no unauthenticated RCE. Realistic ceiling is same-tenant notification-content spoofing or breaking one notification (minor DoS).
findings.rationale:
Confirmed at send_notifications_base.py:43 (Teams) and :65-66 (Slack): notification_message.replace(""", '\"') on a hand-built JSON template string. Django's DjangoTemplates backend has autoescape ON by default and applies to ALL rendered files regardless of extension; only the email .tpl files opt out via {% autoescape off %}, while slack_observation.tpl / msteams_observation.tpl rely on default escaping — confirming autoescape is active on the vulnerable path. Django's escape() handles < > & " ' but leaves backslash untouched. observation.title is core/models.py:251 title = CharField(max_length=255), populated verbatim from untrusted imported scanner reports (e.g. secobserve parser: title=uploaded_observation.get("title")) with no backslash/quote sanitization; low-priv Upload/Writer roles can upload reports per the stated environment. Reachable: send_observation_notification builds first_line embedding observation.title and calls send_msteams_notification (first call-site send_notifications_observation.py:109) and send_slack_notification (:119); msteams_observation.tpl:25 also interpolates observation.title directly into a JSON value. Parity attack verified step-by-step: title foo\"bar -> autoescape -> foo\"bar -> replace "->\" -> foo\\"bar, where \\ is a valid escaped backslash and the following " prematurely terminates the JSON string, breaking out into the Slack/Teams payload structure. Not XSS (rule 14 is about auto-escaped HTML; this is JSON injection into an external system). Not log-spoof/open-redirect nuisance (rule 12): impact is arbitrary JSON structure injection into a cross-team alerting channel (message spoofing, link/field/Block-Kit manipulation), which exceeds a low-impact nuisance and supports the MEDIUM rating. Not test/dead code, not intended behavior — the replace is clearly an attempt at JSON escaping that is simply incomplete. Confidence held below 1.0 because exact runtime escape behavior was reasoned from Django semantics rather than executed (read-only, no exec).

The parity bug is real and confirmed: templates (msteams_observation.tpl, slack_observation.tpl) hand-build JSON with Django HTML autoescape, which escapes double-quotes to " but leaves backslashes untouched; the downstream replace('"', '\\\"') in send_notifications_base.py:43/66 then converts a title-embedded \\\" into \\\\\" = escaped-backslash + bare quote, terminating the JSON string and letting attacker-controlled imported data inject JSON structure. Reachability is genuine (send_notifications_observation.py:109/119). STEP 2: preconditions number 3+ (import role + pre-configured webhook + trigger gate + crafted payload), which lands in the LOW column; access is authenticated, the MEDIUM column; taking the lower gives LOW. STEP 3: no threat-model match because the payload reaches only the same tenant's own configured webhook -- no tenant-to-tenant leak, no priv-esc, no secret/key exposure, no unauth RCE -- so no upward adjustment. The blast radius is content injection/spoofing into the org's own chat channel or a broken notification, all within the originating tenant. STEP 4: the scanner's MEDIUM overstates a contained, same-tenant, multi-precondition, low-impact JSON-injection by one level; score -2. STEP 5: exploitable -- the parity defect is deterministically triggerable by a crafted title once the webhook and trigger preconditions hold. Derived severity: LOW.

findings.title: Unsanitized OpenVEX document_id_prefix reaches Content-Disposition filename
API-token auth loops Argon2 verify over every token in the DB on each request
findings.rationale: The code is exactly as described: _validate_api_token (line 49-59) loads API_Token_Multiple.objects.all() and runs PasswordHasher().verify() against the bearer string per token until a match, no prefix/index narrowing (the model at models.py:154-166 has no prefix column to narrow on), and it runs for any request whose Authorization prefix is "APIToken" since the class is a default global auth backend (base.py:367/373). So the structural claim is true. But the impact rating as HIGH algorithmic-DoS does not hold up adversarially. The per-request cost is O(N) where N = total provisioned tokens system-wide, and N is NOT attacker-controlled within a request: the attacker supplies one bearer string and the work done is a fixed N Argon2 verifications regardless of request content. There is no request-content-driven complexity blowup (no quadratic/exponential explosion from attacker input), which is what distinguishes a genuine algorithmic-complexity vulnerability. Inflating N requires authenticated token creation, bounded by unique_together=(user,name) (models.py:163), so a low-priv attacker cannot grow the multiplier arbitrarily. The only attacker lever is request RATE, and that is exactly what the default AnonRateThrottle (10/s) and UserRateThrottle (100/s) cap (base.py:391-395) — the throttle governs the pre-auth path that reaches this code. Total attack cost = rate x N, i.e. purely the volumetric dimension the throttle already bounds. Running a deliberately-expensive Argon2 hash on a credential-verification path is intended/standard behavior; the linear scan is at most a missing-hardening/efficiency item (a token-prefix index would let it short-circuit) with no concrete disproportionate single-request exploit. This matches exclusion rule 1 (volumetric DoS) and rule 13 (missing-hardening only). Residual uncertainty (confidence 0.78): if an install accumulates a very large N and the anon throttle were misconfigured/removed in production, sustained 10/s requests x large N could still pressure CPU — but that is volumetric and throttle-governed by design, not an algorithmic-complexity HIGH.

Api_Configuration_Create) and put_permission=Api_Configuration_Edit (permissions.py:15-26). findings.title: User-authored Rego policy can read the server process environment via opa.runtime().env (secret exfiltration)
findings.rationale:
The finding's load-bearing claim is that regopy/rego-cpp implements opa.runtime() with an env key that returns the SecObserve process environment, enabling secret exfiltration via a persisted, UI-shown query result. This mechanism is not present in the embedding.

(1) First call-site: rule_engine.py:66 -> RegoInterpreter(rule.rego_module); the constructor (rego_interpreter.py:16) only does Interpreter(); add_module("rule", ...); build("data"). Query side (line 25-27) only sets Input(data) (the observation) and runs the bundle. No env is ever passed in.

(2) The dependency is regopy 1.3.0 = Microsoft rego-cpp (pyproject.toml:77), a from-scratch C++ implementation of the Rego *language*, NOT the OPA Go *server runtime*. I read the full Python binding (.venv/.../regopy/interpreter.py and rego_shared.py): there is no runtime config, no env/getenv injection, nothing that wires os.environ into the native interpreter. grep of rego_shared.py for environ/getenv/runtime/env returns nothing.

(3) In the compiled librego_shared.so the string "opa.runtime" appears once, and the only env-related text is the *OPA documentation string* copied into the builtin descriptor table ("an `env` key containing the environment variables that the OPA process was started with"). The actual getenv/environ symbols are glibc internals (secure_getenv@GLIBC, __environ@GLIBC), not a policy-accessible data source. opa.runtime().env is populated only by OPA's Go server at startup; there is no such runtime here to populate it, so it returns at most an empty/undefined object — not the SecObserve process env.

Auth context (secondary): authoring Rego requires superuser (general rules, permissions.py UserHasGeneralRulePermission) or Product_Rule_Create (Owner/Maintainer-tier per roles_permissions.py), matching the stated trusted-operator surface — but the refutation rests on the missing env mechanism, not merely the auth gate.

Caveat: under the no-exec constraint I cannot run a PoC to definitively show opa.runtime().env returns {}; confidence is bounded by that. However, the complete absence of any env-population path plus the fact that the only supporting evidence is copied upstream documentation text makes the claimed exfiltration implausible as wired.

findings.title: NUL-byte stripping applied only to description; title and sibling fields reach the DB raw (regression of fix 156cb2d6)
findings.rationale: The code mechanism is real and correctly described. observation.py:254 (_normalize_description) replaces � only on description; title and siblings get no NUL cleaning. normalize_observation_fields (observation.py:190) is invoked from the pre_save signal observation_pre_save (signals.py:30) on every Observation save, and from import_observations.py:308. title is set from attacker-controlled parser fields: SARIF parser.py:115/125 (result["ruleId"] -> get_title), gitleaks parser.py:80 (RuleID), cyclonedx parser.py:247. The JSON decoder used at parser_detector.py:45 (json.load) accepts � in string literals, so a NUL survives parsing into title. clip_fields (functions.py:27) only length-truncates, no NUL stripping. On PostgreSQL, .save() (e.g. import_observations.py:718/791) of a text column containing 0x00 raises ValueError, which is not caught in the import service. So a low-priv Upload/Writer can craft a SARIF/gitleaks/CycloneDX report whose rule id contains � and trigger an unhandled exception. HOWEVER the concrete impact is bounded: a single crafted upload yields an HTTP 500 instead of a clean 400 on the attacker's own import, the surrounding save fails so no partial/corrupt state persists, and there is no cross-product leakage, no auth bypass, and no service-wide availability impact (not volumetric, not amplified). This is a missing input-validation / robustness gap whose realized consequence is a low-impact nuisance (malformed-input 500 on the caller's own request), matching exclusion rule 12. The MEDIUM rating overstates impact; the finding is accurate as a hardening note but not actionable as a security vulnerability of that severity.

findings.title: Dependency-Track base_url is a user-set host with no allowlist / internal-range block (read-SSRF)
findings.rationale: Code is exactly as described: parser.py:54 does requests.get on api_configuration.base_url (CharField(max_length=255), no validators — models.py:42) concatenated with a fixed path; no scheme/host/IP/RFC1918 validation, and check_connection returns response.json() (parser.py:64), giving a read oracle. Call chain: ApiConfigurationSerializer.validate (serializers.py:123-162, triggered by test_connection=True) -> api_check_connection (import_observations.py:268-276) -> check_connection. Reachable also via the import path (import_observations.py:217). HOWEVER, the actor who can set base_url and trigger the fetch must hold Api_Configuration_Create/Edit, which authorization/services/roles_permissions.py grants ONLY to Maintainer (lines 249-286) and Owner (298-338) — never Reader/Upload/Writer. The environment brief itself states Maintainer/Owner configure integrations. Fetching a user-supplied integration base_url and returning its findings IS the documented purpose of the API parser feature (reach the operator's own Dependency-Track instance, which is legitimately often on an internal network). No lower-privileged actor crosses a boundary here; the SSRF reaches only the server's network position, exposed to the same trusted role that configures all outbound integrations, and yields no cross-product data (response is the configured project's findings, returned to that operator). This is intended design / trusted-operator input (rules 3 and 8); adding an allowlist would be defense-in-depth hardening (rule 13), not closing a real privilege-crossing exploit. Note: a hardening allowlist/RFC1918 block would still be reasonable defense-in-depth and worth a backlog item, but it does not make this a TRUE_POSITIVE under the given threat model.

findings.title: GitLab PRIVATE-TOKEN sent to a user-controlled base_url with no host validation
findings.rationale: Code claim is accurate: base_issue_tracker.py:84 _normalize_base_url only trims a trailing slash (no scheme/host allowlist, no internal-range block), and gitlab_issue_tracker.py:117 _get_headers attaches PRIVATE-TOKEN on every call to the URL built from product.issue_tracker_base_url; requests follows redirects by default. BUT the security premise fails. base_url and api_key are both set via Product PUT, gated by Permissions.Product_Edit. authorization/services/roles_permissions.py shows Product_Edit (1102) is held only by Maintainer(4) and Owner(5); the Writer role set lacks it, and Upload/Writer cannot edit the product. The environment description itself classifies Maintainer/Owner as the trusted "configure integrations" roles. Crucially, the credential allegedly exposed (issue_tracker_api_key) is entered by the SAME Maintainer/Owner, on the SAME product, in the SAME form (serializers_product.py validate requires base_url+api_key together). The actor pointing base_url at an attacker/internal host is the same actor who owns the token. Each product has its own key (models.py:99-101) with no cross-product sharing, so no other tenant's secret is exposed and no privilege boundary is crossed — the "cross-product access is a breach" condition is not met. This is a trusted-operator configuration input directing the operator's own credential to a host the operator chose: exclusion rule 8 (trusted operator config) and rule 3 (intended integration design, identical to any webhook/SMTP URL field). The redirect angle is SSRF path-only (rule 5) against the operator's own token. Could be reclassified to a minor hardening recommendation (add scheme/host validation), but as a credential-exposure vuln with concrete cross-boundary impact it does not hold. Residual uncertainty: did not exhaustively confirm there is no alternate lower-priv API import path that sets base_url, but the only Product write path found is gated by Product_Edit.

findings.title: JWT_Secret.load() empty-secret regeneration path is broken (latent), no live empty-secret signing
findings.rationale: The bug at models.py:124 (jwt_secret.secret(cls.create_secret()) calling a str as callable) is real but unreachable and fail-closed. The guard at line 123 (if not jwt_secret.secret) can only be true for a persisted row whose secret is empty, but save() at lines 115-116 unconditionally sets secret = create_secret() whenever secret is falsy before super().save(), so no DB row can ever have an empty secret. The buggy branch is therefore dead. Even if reached, it raises TypeError, making load() throw — authentication fails closed; it never proceeds with a weak, empty, or predictable secret. create_secret() uses secrets.choice over a 62-char alphabet x 32 chars, which is strong. Callers (create_jwt at jwt_authentication.py:31, _validate_jwt at :69) always receive a non-empty random HS256 secret. The finding itself concedes "the secret is never empty" and labels it "a fragile invariant" — i.e., a latent code-quality bug with no concrete exploit, not a weak-crypto vulnerability. Matches exclusion rule 13 (missing-hardening / fragile invariant only, no demonstrable exploit).

findings.title: No account lockout on password auth; unauthenticated login/token-mint endpoints brute-forceable
findings.rationale: Structurally the finding is accurate: AuthenticateView (views.py:318), UserAPITokenCreateView (:266) and UserAPITokenRevokeView (:295) all set authentication_classes=[]/permission_classes=[] and route username+password through _get_authenticated_user -> django_authenticate (:354). They are live, unauthenticated, public routes (config/urls.py:75-81). INSTALLED_APPS/AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS (base.py:141) contain only ModelBackend - no django-axes, no defender, no ratelimit, no failed-attempt counter, no per-view throttle override. So account lockout genuinely does not exist. However this is missing-hardening-only with no concrete exploit (rule 13): (1) an existing IP-keyed AnonRateThrottle at 10/second (base.py:391-395) caps online guessing; (2) passwords are Argon2-hashed (:155) with the full Django validator set - MinimumLength, CommonPassword blocklist, Numeric, UserAttributeSimilarity (:163-168) - making online brute-force of any policy-compliant password infeasible even at distributed rates; (3) the asserted "one-call token mint" still requires already-valid credentials, so the only attack is online password guessing, which succeeds solely against a weak/known password (a deployment choice, not a code defect). Account lockout is a defense-in-depth control whose absence is also a defensible design tradeoff (lockout itself enables account-lockout DoS), so the team relying on rate-limit + strong hashing is intentional and reasonable. No concrete, code-level exploit is demonstrated; the class is real but not actionable as a vulnerability.
first_links: backend/application/access_control/api/views.py:327 (AuthenticateView.post calls _get_authenticated_user); the shared sink is _get_authenticated_user at views.py:354 calling django_authenticate; same sink reached from UserAPITokenCreateView.post:279 and UserAPITokenRevokeView.post:308
backend/config/urls.py:75 (api/authentication/authenticate/ -> AuthenticateView.as_view()); token mint at urls.py:81 -> UserAPITokenCreateView

findings.title: Committed default admin/admin credentials auto-create a superuser at deploy time
findings.rationale:
Mechanics confirmed: docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:69 is ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin}, so unless the operator exports SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD the container env ADMIN_PASSWORD is the literal "admin" (never empty). The entrypoint (docker/backend/prod/django/entrypoint:28-32) only fires its /dev/urandom random-password fallback when ADMIN_PASSWORD is empty, so via this compose layer that branch indeed never fires and a superuser admin/admin is auto-created on first boot (entrypoint:39-43, gated by the existence check at line 23-24). The finding's chain is accurate.

However this is an operator-overridable default in a deployment template, not a hardcoded secret baked into shipped product code. docs/getting_started/installation.md:3-5 explicitly labels both prod compose files as "templates for productive use only" that "will need proper configuration ... including additional hardening and security measures," and lines 32-34 explicitly list SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD among values that "should be changed for productive use, to avoid using the default values for secrets." The config is bound to *.localhost hosts (compose lines 62-63, 83), i.e. a local template, and the documented override (export SO_ADMIN_PASSWORD before docker compose up) is a trusted-operator env input that fully suppresses the default. The credential is supplied by, and controllable by, the deploying operator — not committed as a fixed secret in the application.

This is intended/documented template behavior (exclusion rule 3) driven by trusted-operator env input (exclusion rule 8). The "hardcoded-secret" class does not fit: the value is a placeholder default the operator is instructed to replace, with an entrypoint random fallback as additional safety. Voting FALSE_POSITIVE.

findings.title: Unsanitized user-controlled document_id_prefix injected into Content-Disposition filename (CycloneDX)
findings.rationale:
Data flow is real: serializers.py:190 document_id_prefix = CharField(max_length=255) has no character/regex validator, flows unquoted into the Content-Disposition filename at views.py:447 via the BOM "prefix" property and _get_cyclonedx_vex_filename (views.py:640-650). So the static observation is accurate. But the vulnerable CLASS does not hold:

1) Dangerous form (HTTP response splitting / header injection) is blocked by the framework. The target runs Django 6.0.5 (backend/pyproject.toml:14), whose HttpResponseBase.__setitem__ raises BadHeaderError on any CR/LF in a header value. The finding itself concedes this. CR/LF-based splitting, cache poisoning, and second-header injection are therefore not achievable — already_handled by Django.

2) Residual claim ("parameter injection / filename override" via quotes/semicolons/spaces) has no concrete exploit. The flow is entirely self-targeted: the attacker supplies document_id_prefix in their own POST body (create_cyclonedx_document at cyclonedx_generator.py:62 returns the Bom directly to the requesting caller; views.py:434-448 streams it back synchronously) and is the sole recipient of the response. There is no path where one user's prefix is reflected into a DIFFERENT user's Content-Disposition — the update path (views.py:457, update_cyclonedx_document:114) also returns the doc only to the VEX_Edit-authorized caller. Manipulating the filename of one's own download crosses no privilege/trust boundary and yields no cross-product or cross-user breach.

This leaves only a self-inflicted cosmetic filename quirk with no demonstrable victim — missing input hardening without a concrete exploit (exclusion 13), and at most a low-impact nuisance (exclusion 12). Severity LOW is generous; net assessment is non-actionable / false positive.
first_links: backend/application/vex/api/views.py:402 (CycloneDXDocumentCreateView.post) -> views.py:429 builds CycloneDXCreateParameters(document_id_prefix=serializer.validated_data) -> services/cyclonedx_generator.py:96/167 _add_metadata sets Property(name="prefix", value=document_id_prefix) -> views.py:640 _get_cyclonedx_vex_filename embeds prefix in filename -> views.py:447 Content-Disposition

findings.title: Whole uploaded report parsed into memory with no content-size cap before walking
findings.rationale:
Code confirmed: parser_detector.py:45 is `data = load(file)` (full json.load into RAM); CSV path (lines 27-37) reads the whole file and builds a `rows` list. No DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE / FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE override exists in the backend (config/settings/* and the import_observations app), and the serializer's FileField(max_length=255) bounds only the filename, not content. The path is reachable by authenticated low-priv (Upload) users via file_upload_observations (import_observations.py:128). So the factual claim is accurate.

However, the vulnerability class is plain volumetric DoS, which is an explicit exclusion (rule 1). Despite the "algorithmic-dos" label, the described attack is "POST a multi-hundred-MB JSON/CSV loaded into RAM" — resource consumption proportional to attacker-supplied size. No superlinear amplification exists: json.load is O(n), the CSV row loop is O(n), _get_parser calls each parser's check_format once (linear, not nested over the data), and the json.dumps-into-evidence step scales linearly with entry count/size. There is no quadratic/exponential blowup, no decompression-bomb-style multiplier — a 200 MB upload costs O(200 MB) of memory, not more. This is "big upload uses big memory," i.e. volumetric DoS, which exclusion rule 1 removes. Confidence below 1.0 only because a missing global body-size cap is a legitimate hardening gap; but per the exclusion ruleset it is not an actionable finding of the claimed class.

findings.title: Jira client uses a user-controlled server URL with basic_auth credentials, no host validation
findings.rationale:
Code is exactly as described: jira_issue_tracker.py:18-24 constructs JIRA(server=product.issue_tracker_base_url, basic_auth=(username, api_key)) and serializers_product.py:377-393 validate() only checks field presence, no scheme/host allowlist or internal-range block. First call-site: issue_tracker_factory at issue_tracker/services/issue_tracker.py:94 (reached via push_observations_to_issue_tracker, views_product.py:365 / import_observations.py:356).

But the security framing fails on the trust model. Both issue_tracker_base_url AND the credentials (issue_tracker_username/issue_tracker_api_key) live on the same Product record, written together in one update guarded by UserHasProductPermission -> Permissions.Product_Edit (core/api/permissions.py:33). Product_Edit is granted ONLY to Roles.Maintainer and Roles.Owner (authorization/services/roles_permissions.py:253,303) -- exactly the operators the environment names as 'configure integrations'. Upload/Writer (the untrusted-report uploaders) cannot set these fields.

So the SAME trusted operator supplies both the destination URL and the credential being sent there. There is no privilege boundary crossed and no cross-product breach: nobody is redirecting a third party's credential -- an operator points their own API key at a server they themselves chose. That is the designed function of configuring an outbound issue-tracker integration (exclusion 8: trusted operator config input; reinforced by exclusion 3: intended design). The 'no host allowlist / SSRF-to-internal-range' angle is hardening-only (exclusion 13) and, even if pursued, would be SSRF-path-only by a trusted operator against a self-chosen target (exclusion 5) with no escalation. Scanner's MEDIUM credential-exposure characterization treats an operator-to-operator-controlled flow as an attacker-controlled redirect, which is the misjudgment.

findings.title: No CPU/time/memory budget around Rego evaluation of untrusted policies
findings.rationale:
CONFIRMED MECHANISM: rego_interpreter.py:23 query() calls rego_run.query_bundle synchronously (line 27) with no timeout, step cap, or memory ceiling, on rule.rego_module content. First call site: rule_engine.py:284 (result = rego_interpreter.query(observation_dict)); the interpreter is instantiated at rule_engine.py:66 from rule.rego_module.

WHY FALSE_POSITIVE: This is an algorithmic-DoS class finding (exclusion rule 1), and the assumed attacker model does not hold.

(1) Attacker authority: The rego_module is attacker-AUTHORED only by trusted operators. Authoring a product rego rule requires Permissions.Product_Rule_Create, granted ONLY to Maintainer (roles_permissions.py:267) and Owner (line 318). The low-priv roles named in the environment — Upload (only Product_Import_Observations) and Writer (Product_Rule_VIEW only, no create) — cannot author rego. General rules require is_superuser (permissions.py:26). So no low-priv or cross-product actor can inject Rego source.

(2) The "approval workflow" the finding leans on is self-administered and not a real barrier: product rules default to AUTO_APPROVED unless product.product_rules_need_approval is set (models.py:84-99), and the same Maintainer/Owner who authors the rule also holds Product_Rule_Approval (line 269) and configures the need-approval flag. So the gate is opt-in, not "heavily gated" — but it confirms the author is a trusted operator with full configuration authority over that product.

(3) Impact: a privileged, in-scope operator writing a deliberately expensive Rego policy that burns CPU/RAM during their own product's rule-apply loop is a self-inflicted resource-exhaustion by a trusted actor. No privilege boundary is crossed, no cross-product access (the engine scopes rules to the operator's own product, rule_engine.py:35-61). The simulate endpoint (views.py:135) runs an already-created rule, so it does not lower the authoring bar.

This matches exclusion rule 1 (volumetric/algorithmic DoS) and rule 3/8 (intended design / trusted-operator input). Real code behavior, wrong threat actor. Residual uncertainty: regopy may impose its own internal limits (not verifiable read-only without the C library), and an org could legitimately worry about a compromised Maintainer credential — hence not full confidence — but under the stated threat model this is not an actionable cross-trust vuln.

findings.title: VEX document create/update views rely on default IsAuthenticated; per-product check only when product is set
findings.rationale:
The code claim is mechanically accurate (not a misread): CycloneDXDocumentCreateView.post (views.py:402) declares no permission_classes, so DRF falls back to the global DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES = IsAuthenticated (settings/base.py:386). The VEX_Create check at views.py:408-409 is guarded by `if product:`, so when a request supplies only vulnerability_names the VEX_Create permission is never enforced. Call-site: config/urls.py:143 -> CycloneDXDocumentCreateView.as_view().

However the finding is not an exploitable broken-access-control issue. The no-product path builds the document via _create_vulnerabilities -> get_observations_for_vulnerabilities (vex_base.py:80-83), which is `get_observations().filter(vulnerability_id__in=...)`. get_observations() (observation.py:27-63) hard-scopes the base queryset for any non-superuser to products where the user is a Product_Member / product-group member / authorization-group member (the Q() membership filter at lines 56-61). The generated VEX therefore can only ever contain observations the caller can already read; there is no cross-product/cross-tenant disclosure (the environment's breach condition) and no write effect on other products (the created CycloneDX row has product=None).

Net: a user who can already READ a product's observations but lacks the VEX_Create role can still emit a VEX artifact over data they already see. That is a missing authorization gate with no concrete confidentiality, integrity, or cross-product impact beyond the attacker's existing access -- defense-in-depth / authorization-completeness only. Matches exclusion rule 13 (missing-hardening-only, no concrete exploit). The finding's own text concedes the impact is bounded by the authorization-scoped query. Confidence is not higher only because the gate is genuinely absent, so a reviewer wanting strict role-completeness could still want it added; it just is not an exploitable vuln.

findings.title: Gitleaks secret redaction is a literal substring replace; mismatched Secret/Match can leave the secret stored
findings.rationale: Code confirmed: line 67 does `match = match.replace(secret, "REDACTED")`, literal substring replace, and the no-op-on-mismatch behavior described is real. But the exploit premise collapses under the trust model. The only actor who can produce a Match/Secret mismatch is the uploader of the gitleaks JSON (untrusted input at import_observations.py:145), and the only "secret" that could persist is a string the uploader themselves placed in their own report. There is no other party's secret to leak. Crucially, redaction is applied ONLY to the Match field; the `description` field (parser.py:54, from entry.get("Description")) plus Message, File, Commit, etc. are stored verbatim with zero redaction. An uploader wanting to expose an arbitrary string to other product viewers can simply put it in Description — no mismatch trick needed. So the claimed primitive grants no capability the uploader doesn't already have, and produces no cross-product or cross-privilege exposure. For genuine gitleaks output the tool guarantees Secret is an exact substring of Match, so redaction works as designed (intended-behavior). This is at most missing-hardening with no concrete exploit (rule 13); it is also arguably intended design relying on the documented gitleaks Secret-in-Match invariant (rule 3). LOW severity self-exposure of attacker-owned data is not actionable.

findings.title: Email notification templates disable autoescaping on import-derived title/product/description
findings.rationale:
Confirmed by reading the file: email_observation.tpl:1 uses {% autoescape off %} and interpolates observation.title / product.name / first_line. First call-site is send_notifications_observation.py:97-105 -> send_email_notification(...). That function (send_notifications_base.py:23-29) calls Django send_mail with message= only and NO html_message; grep for html_message/EmailMultiAlternatives/attach_alternative/content_subtype across the backend returns nothing, so emails are unambiguously plain-text. The finding correctly concedes this is not stored-XSS.

The finding's named root cause is wrong: it pins the issue on `autoescape off`, but autoescape only governs HTML-entity escaping (< > & " '), which is irrelevant and undesirable in a plain-text email (escaping would inject literal "/& strings into mails). Autoescape does NOT escape newlines, so the claimed multi-line/newline-injection "content spoofing" would occur identically whether autoescape is on or off. The protection it flags as missing has no causal link to the claimed impact -- a misread of how the mechanism works; autoescape-off is the intended, correct choice for a plaintext template.

The residual real impact is only that an attacker who controls an observation title (CharField max_length 255; Django does not strip newlines) could embed newlines that add extra plain-text lines (e.g. a fake "Severity:") into a notification email whose recipient already receives that title as displayable content. No HTML/markup execution, no privilege escalation, no cross-product access, no concrete security consequence -- a plain-text content/log-spoof-class nuisance. Matches exclusion rule 12 (low-impact nuisance: content/log spoofing) and the protection it flags is intended behavior for plaintext (also rule 13: missing-hardening-only, no concrete exploit). FALSE_POSITIVE.

findings.title: Unbounded recursion over attacker-nested CycloneDX components
findings.rationale: The recursion at parser.py:166-167 (_get_sbom_component_with_subs calling itself per nested "components" level, no depth cap) is real. But the parser only ever runs on a dict already produced by stdlib json.load. Tracing back: _get_sbom_component_with_subs is called from _get_components (parser.py:145) and _get_root_component_with_subs (parser.py:158); _get_components is reached via get_observations/get_license_components, which receive `data` from import_observations.py (145/194/221), which gets it from detect_parser -> parser_detector.py:45 `data = load(file)` (from json import load). CPython's json.load enforces a recursion limit and raises on deeply nested documents; parser_detector.py:46-47 catches any such exception and re-raises it as DRF ValidationError ("File is not valid JSON"), returning HTTP 400. To overflow the ~1000-frame Python limit in _get_sbom_component_with_subs you need ~1000 nested components, i.e. ~2000 JSON nesting levels, which json.load rejects first. So a document that parses successfully has bounded nesting and the walk is bounded by the same limit. Worst case for an oversized-but-parseable doc is CPU/time on a single request (volumetric DoS) or a caught RecursionError — Python is memory-safe, no corruption. This matches exclusion rule 1 (volumetric/algorithmic DoS) and is additionally neutralized by the upstream json.load bound the finding itself acknowledges. The finding even rates itself 1/3 votes and LOW.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled report text rendered as markdown in observation description (framework-mitigated)
findings.rationale: Line 284-295 do concatenate attacker-controlled SARIF result.properties / rule.properties into the markdown `description` (and the description is stored raw — no backend bleach/escape, confirmed). So the SOURCE is real and untrusted (low-priv Upload/Writer can upload SARIF). But XSS requires the SINK to execute markup, and it does not. The description is rendered by frontend/src/commons/custom_fields/MarkdownField.tsx via markdown-to-jsx 9.8.1 (frontend/package.json:23). That component passes ONLY `overrides` for `a`/`code` — no `sanitizer` override, no `createElement` override, no raw-HTML-enabling option — and there is zero `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` anywhere in frontend/src (grep clean). I inspected the installed library bytes (node_modules/markdown-to-jsx/dist/index.cjs): the default sanitizer is `var M6=/(javascript|vbscript|data(?!:image)):/i` applied to `href`/`src` props (`(F==="href"||F==="src")&&Z?.sanitizer`), with HTML-entity decode (s9) and percent-decode normalization before re-testing, defeating common scheme-obfuscation bypasses; and `tagfilter` defaults on (`tagfilter:Q?.tagfilter!==!1`), stripping `<script>/<iframe>/<style>` etc. markdown-to-jsx converts any surviving inline HTML to React elements, so string event-handler attributes (onerror/onclick) are not executed by React. Every injection path (raw script tag, javascript:/vbscript:/data: URL in a link/image, event-handler attribute) is closed by a default framework control with no escape hatch enabled. This is textbook exclusion rule 14 (XSS in auto-escape framework, no raw-HTML escape hatch). Confidence capped below 1.0 because the mitigation depends on the markdown-to-jsx default sanitizer/tagfilter not being disabled and on the pinned 9.8.1 version — a future config change adding a createElement/sanitizer override or a dependency bump weakening defaults would reopen it (defense-in-depth: also bleach the description server-side). The finding's own LOW rating and "framework-mitigated near-FP" wording already concede this.
